## KEY MESSAGES

We upgrade our 2026 and 2027 aluminium price forecasts:We lift our end-2026 price expectations by USD200/t due to deteriorating supply growth and a tighter market. We also upgrade our H1 2027 forecast but leave our already bullish end2027 target unchanged.

Limited supply growth: The market should tighten in 2026-27, even allowing for slower demand, due to China reaching its self-imposed production cap, slow Indonesian capacity build-out and ramp-up, as well as smelter closures or outages (Mozal, Grundartangi). We expect a global deficit of at least 431kt this year, rising to more than 600kt in 2027, with tightening fundamentals and time spreads supporting prices.

## Heavy fund flows since November have added to the price-positive narrative:

Speculative net long positions in LME aluminium reached record highs in January 2026, as part of a wider rotation into metals from the energy complex. We see growing speculative interest in hard-asset exposure as a result of heightened geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty.

Deeper backwardation beckons in LME forward curve: Near-term (cash-to3month) and longer-dated (3-15month) LME aluminium spreads have narrowed since the 'Liberation Day' tariff shock on 2 April 2025. While spreads have eased into February, we expect growing physical tightness to push the market into deeper backwardation in 2026.

Risks: We see the main risks to our expectations as: 1) uncertainty about US tariff policy; 2) greater risk of geopolitical shocks; and 3) a relaxation or slippage of China's 45Mt/year production cap.

Spot-on: These forecasts build on the views we set out in our aluminium outlook last year, when we correctly flagged limited aluminium supply growth, upside in physical premiums and ongoing backwardation (see appendix).

## Investors surged into aluminium in November on positive fundamentals

LME aluminium speculative net length at record highs in January; we think this is a positive underlying supply narrative, while macro cues have also driven interest

Second part of report title Ongoing price-supporting fundamentals attract fund flows: A positive price supportive supply story for aluminium has been building for a while, as we projected in January 2025. From November 2025, we started to see the fund communitybuying into the supply-constrained tightening narrative for aluminium.

China's cap on domestic aluminium production has been key to changing aluminium market: China's 45Mt/year production cap was effectively reached in 2025. This, plus a much slower build-out and ramp-up of Chinese backed Indonesian smelter capacity, has materially changed market dynamics, bringing supply constraint back as an issue supporting aluminium prices for the first time since the early 2000s.

Build-out of Indonesian capacity slower and more challenging than previously expected: Chinese-financed smelter capacity in Indonesia was supposed to offset the impact of China's own domestic supply cap but this has not occurred. Three new smelters have been built, only one of which, the Tsingshan/Xinfa JV Kemajuan plant, is operating; the Adaro smelter starts operation this year and Nanshan does not start until the end of 2027/early2028.

Longer-dated LME aluminium time spreads have narrowed since April 2024, in our view driven by tightening market fundamentals, an appealing narrative for investors

## Demand outlook challenging; trade protectionism still a threat

Manufacturing activity is struggling globally, with PMIs at or below the key 50-point level in all major regions

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Source: Bloomberg, BNP Paribas

In contrast, Chinese passenger car output grew by 10% in 2025, driven by exports largely to other Asian markets, Latam and Europe; domestic sales were flat y/y

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Sources: Bloomberg, BNP Paribas

Second part of report title Global manufacturing struggling to grow: Manufacturing purchasing manager indices (PMIs) in key Western economic blocs are all below 50, with activity in the US starting to contract sharply. While we see benefits from ongoing growth of Chinese demand, we also see a rising risk that this demand mayfalter.

Ex-China demand to remain sluggish in 2026: We forecast ex-China aluminium demand to grow by 1.2% in 2026. In the US, we still see sluggish primary demand, notably driven by the negative demand impact from tariffs. In Europe, while sentiment should be boosted by increased infrastructure and defence spending, we remain concerned about demand from the European auto sector.

China trends vital to global demand: Demand from Chinese manufacturing accounts for just under 60% of global primary aluminium demand (about 43.5Mt). Construction and infrastructure account for some 30% of Chinese demand, while export-focused transport, consumer goods, packaging and industrial equipment account for about 70%. We see energy infrastructure demand and demand from export-focused sectors, offsetting the weaker construction demand, but note the exposure to export-focused sectors presents a risk to our demand and price outlook for 2025, in the face of rising trade tensionswith theUS.

Chinese air conditioner production, at 268mn units, only grew 0.6% y/y; exports struggled through 2025, contracting 5% y/y

Second part of report title We do not envisage any strong pickup in demand ex-China in 2026, with the US the main drag: We see little prospect of a recovery in manufacturing and construction activity in key ex-China markets in 2026-27. However, we see a switch to better demand in Europe, but slower demand growth in the US.

European auto sector outlook still challenging but some signs of improvement: Auto registrations showed modest growth through 2025, up 1.5% y/y. Consensus expectations are for this to jump to about 2.9% in 2026. More importantly for metals demand, order intake for European auto manufacturers improved through H2 2025, thanks to auto inventories being drawn down, we think - a trend we expect to continue.

Europe construction activity has been beset by problems: European construction has been contracting since April 2025, but we see clear signs of the down-trend bottoming out. Indeed, we note some signs of improving optimism on pan-European pledges to increase infrastructure and defence spending.

New order intake for the European auto sector was in contraction between June 2023 and October 2024. But we now seen signs of modest recovery for 2026

## Uncertainty over US economic policy remains elevated

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Sources: Bloomberg, BNP Paribas

Second part of report title US consumer sentiment collapsed during 2025: Positive consumer sentiment at the end of 2024 and in early 2025 fed through to stronger US consumer demand for autos and electronics, among other items, in Q1 2025. However, consumer sentiment collapsed during 2025 on fears of rising living costs.

US vehicle sales peaked in Q1 2025 on a combination of Trump optimism and later in the quarter as buyers sought to get ahead of potential tariff effects. However, full-year 2025 sales growth slowed to 2.4% from 3.6% in 2024, with Q4 sales contracting by 3.6% y/y. We now see consumer sentiment faltering, facing a deteriorating jobs market, tariff dis ruption and cos t-of-living headwinds.

US manufacturing, construction start to struggle: US manufacturing has been in contractionary territory since February 2022. Automotive output is struggling with reciprocal tariffs while construction activity (in terms of housing starts) has contracted sharply since July 2025 - completions have been falling since February 2025. We see the packaging and beverage sectors as most impacted by50% aluminium tariffs .

Energy transition demand set to slow in 2026: We expect US energy-transitionrelated demand to have remained robust in 2025, as many projects have been approved and are in development. However, we expect demand to slow in 2026, largely due to Trump administration rollbacks of some Biden IRApolicy measures.

## DEMAND

## China: Stable demand, flat production, more imports, fewer exports

China's renewable sector was a key driver of demand growth in 2024. We had expected this to slow moderately in 2025, with the removal of subsidies, but production grew by about 23% in the year.

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Sources: Bloomberg, BNP Paribas

Demand from new energy, electric vehicles and the tech sector has more than countered the impact of the ongoing contraction in construction-related demand

Second part of report title China imported 2.55Mt of primary in 2025, up 20%y/y: China's full-year 2025 primary aluminium demand growth was 2.8% (about 1.2Mt), down from 3.7% (1.4Mt) in 2024, as the slowdown in construction was offset by strong demand for transport, consumer goods and renewable energy. In 2026, we expect a slowing in demand growth to 2.0% (900Kt), on a likely slowing in solar demand, plus the domestic impact of fewer aluminium semi-fabricated product exports. However, we also forecast almost no Chinese domestic supply growth in 2026, which will lead to a tightening of the Chinese market. Indeed, we expect China's import demand to grow again this year.

Chinese import demand a key tightening factor : We expect China's ongoing demand for imports to help tighten the ex-China market, and to drive continued draw-downs from LME inventory. Currently cash-to-3m spreads have slipped back into contango of c.USD33/t as of 18 February2026, but we expect this to tighten through H1-26. Longerdated 3-to-15-month spreads are in a backwardation of around USD17/t.

Dual risk: We see two main risks to a positive price outlook: 1) Chinese authorities relax the mandated 45Mt/t operational smelter capacity cap (although we see a relaxation as extremely unlikely given regional power consumption targets); and 2) tariff policy uncertainty driving a more severe impact on global demand growth.

## Aluminium balance: No sign of any meaningful supply growth

rapid growth of AI data centre-related power demand. In addition, tariff uncertainty is still a significant barrier to long-term smelter investment. Media reports on 16 February 2026 hinted that the Trump administration was planning to roll back aluminium tariffs that are, in our view, negatively impacting US aluminium demand. Though the stories of roll-back were rebuffed by the White House, they add to uncertainty over whether the tariffs will still be in place by the endof the currentadministration or continued by the next.

Second part of report title Slow Indonesia smelter build-out drives Chinese investment elsewhere: While three new smelters in Indonesia are either built or in-build, progress has been dramatically slower than the typical build and ramp-up time scales in China. This appears to be prompting a pickup in investment elsewhere by Chinese companies, including in Angola and Saudi Arabia. While Angola's small (120kt/y) Huatong smelter project should start in H2 2026, the Shandong Innovation Group 500kt project in Yanbu, Saudi Arabia will not, in our view, be in production until well after 2028.

We remain sceptical about US smelter capacity growth: The main objective of the 50% section 232 tariffs on US primary aluminium imports was to incentivise the development of US smelting capacity. US aluminium production dropped from about 6Mt/y in the early 2000s to about 670kt last year, with only four operating smelters, down from 22 plants at the start of this century. The main issue is high power prices and a lack of base load power availability, which we see deteriorating with the scrapping of renewable energy projects, combined with the Large deficit expected in 2026 and 2027: The significant slowdown in primary aluminium supply growth we project for 2026, and only a modest uptick in 2027 are key to our expectations for a tightening and price-supportive market. Clearly a major risk to this expectation is China continuing its 45Mt/year production cap. China's monthly annualised production rates pushed above 45Mt/y in five out of 12 months last year, suggesting that if this occurs more consistently, it could see China produce closer to 46Mt with no capacity additions.

Aluminium supply-demand balance moved into deficit in H2 2025; we expect balances to tighten further in 2026 and 2027 on limited supply growth

Second part of report title

OVERVIEW

## Aluminium outlook: Tighter and tighter

## KEY MESSAGES

Limited supply growth in 2025/6. The impact of China's production, plus limited ex-China capacity growth, will tighten the market in 2025 even in a slower demand environment. We expect a global deficit of at least 305kt this year, with tightening fundamentals and tightening time spreads providing modest price support.

Removal of VAT rebates on aluminium semis exports from China to add to market tightness: The Chinese Ministry of Finance announced the removal of the 13% VAT rebate on aluminium semi exports effective from December 1st 2024 to try and counter the domestic impact of China's capped aluminium production. We expect lower semis exports through 2025, which will tighten the ex-China aluminium market.

We see upside in physical premiums globally through 2025: Over the last year, the US mid-west, Rotterdam duty-paid, and delivered Shanghai premiums have rallied by 33%, 80% and 108% respectively on tightening physical markets. We expect a tightening physical market through 2025 to continue to support premiums, with US premiums seeing further upside from US import tariffs.

Backwardation beckons in LME forward curve: Nearby (cash -3m) and longer dated (3-15 m) LME aluminium spreads have been tightening consistently since August 2024. We expect growing physical tightness to push the market into backwardation through H1-25.

Stronger USD no headwind to aluminium: We expect physical aluminium tightness to cushion aluminium against our expectation of a strong USD through 2025.

Risks: 1) We see key risks to our expectations being a rapid implementation of an aggressive tariff policy from the incoming Trump presidency leading to significantly lower rates of global growth. 2) A relaxation of China's 45 Mt/year aluminium production cap.
